text: The seven tenets from last lesson describe what a Zero Trust Architecture has to accomplish. This lesson names the three components NIST SP 800-207 actually defines to accomplish it — the Policy Engine, the Policy Administrator, and the Policy Enforcement Point. Once you can name these three and tell them apart, you can look at almost any access control you've already configured and say exactly which role it's playing.

The Policy Engine is the decision-maker — it runs a trust algorithm and outputs grant, deny, or revoke for a subject trying to reach a resource. The Policy Administrator acts on that decision: it establishes or shuts down the actual communication path and issues the session-specific token. NIST groups those two together as the Policy Decision Point, the "brain." The Policy Enforcement Point is separate — the gate that physically sits between subject and resource, enabling, monitoring, and terminating the connection based on what it's told.

The Policy Engine's trust algorithm isn't just a password check. NIST describes it pulling in a Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation system, threat intelligence feeds, network and system activity logs, data access policy, a PKI, an identity management system, and SIEM data — combining signals you've already built in earlier courses into one decision instead of leaving each as a separate, disconnected check.

You were already running pieces of this before today. Azure AD Conditional Access's evaluation engine behaves like a combined PE and PA — evaluating signals and issuing the resulting token. A ZTNA gateway, a SASE edge, or an AWS Verified Access endpoint behaves like a PEP, sitting directly on the connection path. Even an NSG or a service-mesh sidecar enforcing mTLS can act as a PEP at a narrower scope.

What's new isn't the controls — it's being able to point at one of them and say precisely which of the three roles it's playing, and where the gaps still are. Next lesson closes this chapter with a glossary built the same way: every remaining Zero Trust term connected to something you already know how to configure.
